metadata.title: Machine Learning for SERS: From a Draft to a Real Paper
metadata.note: A chronological account of turning a hollow, AI-generated literature-review draft into a rigorously cited research paper: the guidelines that forced every section to explain rather than define, the two-week research-then-rewrite cycle repeated across five weeks, and the specific citation, data-leakage, and honesty fixes that resulted.

beats.narration_text: This is Liam, in for Kumar Karthik. You took a hollow, AI-generated literature review and turned it into something with real citations, honest gaps, and an actual argument. Walk me through what that rewrite actually looked like, week by week.

props.segment: Machine Learning for SERS: From a Draft to a Real Paper
props.command: Walk me through how you rewrote the SERS machine learning review paper, week by week.
output: the first draft was AI-generated and hollow
a guidelines document forced every section to explain, not just define
five weeks, two people, one repeating cycle

beats.narration_text: The first draft looked finished. It covered every method, cosmic ray removal, baseline correction, all of it. But every section only defined its topic. It never said why any of it mattered, or what to actually do with it. Closing that gap between defining and explaining is what five weeks of rewriting was actually spent on.

props.text:
The first draft was complete.
Wait, it was actually hollow.
It defined every term and explained nothing.

beats.narration_text: The original draft was AI generated, and it showed. Sections read like a glossary, cosmic ray removal is this, baseline correction is this, with no thread connecting one idea to the next. Worse, several references either did not exist or did not say what the draft claimed they said. Before any science could be fixed, the structure itself needed a plan.

a warning flag appears labeled citations missing or fake

production_viz.label: the original draft's structural problem
production_viz.mechanic: disconnected sections, broken flow, unreliable references

beats.narration_text: So the team built a guidelines document. Not a style guide, a set of forced questions. Every section had to answer three things: what has actually been done, why does it work or fail, and what do we recommend based on the evidence. A section that only defined a term without answering those three questions was not finished.
beats.new_visual_element: A checklist card with three questions and checkmarks

show.event: a card appears
three questions appear one at a time with checkmarks
kicker labels the rule

production_viz.label: the guidelines document's forced questions
production_viz.mechanic: three-question checklist every section must answer

beats.narration_text: The introduction went to the project manager first, since it needed chemistry background neither of us had, then we layered in the machine learning framing ourselves. From there the sections split. My teammate took two-point-one through two-point-three, and three-point-one through three-point-two. I took two-point-four through two-point-six, and three-point-three through three-point-five.

production_viz.label: how the paper's sections were divided

beats.narration_text: Each section ran on the same two-week rhythm. Week one was spent hunting down every citation, checking whether a claim was actually backed by what its source said. Week two was rewriting, using whatever week one turned up. That cycle ran twice, once per section, across five weeks total, real meetings, real research hours, logged the whole way through.

beats.narration_text: Two-point-four was written from scratch, with real citations for both alignment methods, and an honest caveat that alignment itself can introduce error if the reference spectrum is chosen badly. Two-point-five needed something stronger, the warning that PCA has to be fit only on training data, never the full dataset before splitting. Skip that rule and your test set leaks backward into training. That section also previews a point the deep learning section leans on later, automatic feature learning needs far more data than hand-built features before it's actually worth using.

production_viz.mechanic: two flow diagrams contrasting wrong vs correct PCA fitting order
production_viz.note: real citations named (Savorani 2010, Liu 2017), no invented numbers

beats.narration_text: SERS has its own specific headaches. Hot spots vary randomly from measurement to measurement, usually treated as noise to average away. But one 2025 study trained on deliberately varied hot-spot conditions instead of identical ones, and cut prediction error by eighty-four point eight percent. Separately, a cross-lab study measuring the same samples on thirty-five instruments across fifteen institutes found real, systematic differences that had nothing to do with chemistry, just the hardware. Two very different problems, two real numbers, both added to back up claims that had none before.

the varied bar is much shorter, labeled -84.8% error
citation lines appear for both studies

production_viz.label: hot-spot variability reframed as signal
production_viz.mechanic: bar comparison of error rates, plus cross-instrument calibration citation
production_viz.note: real numbers (84.8% error reduction, 35 instruments/15 institutes), real citations

beats.narration_text: Ensembling, combining several models' predictions, sounds like a free win. It only actually is one when the models fail in different ways. One study combined four classifiers and beat every one of them individually, hitting ninety-seven point nine percent. But another combined just two models and did worse than either alone, because the two classifiers kept disagreeing over noisy data instead of complementing each other. And two textbook models, decision trees and logistic regression, don't get their own sections here at all, because in this literature they only ever show up as pieces inside somebody else's ensemble.

note about decision trees and logistic regression appears

production_viz.label: when ensembling helps vs hurts
production_viz.mechanic: two side-by-side scenarios with real accuracy numbers
production_viz.note: real numbers (97.9%, 97.4%, 76.1%), the SVM+XGBoost case labeled as a preprint

beats.narration_text: The original draft stated the gap as a specific number, reported accuracy overestimates real deployment performance by ten to thirty percentage points. Nobody could find where that number came from. It got removed, replaced with the honest version, this has never actually been measured. The claim that no study has reached the top validation tier got the same honesty treatment, scoped explicitly to the actual databases and years searched, instead of stated as a fact about the entire field.

props.text:
The gap is exactly known.
Wait, that number was never measured.
It's actually unknown, and that's a real research gap.

beats.narration_text: The summary table had its own quiet mistake. A random forest study sitting in the SERS row had never touched Raman spectroscopy at all, it was fecal-source testing, included only because it used the same algorithm. It came out. A long-open citation gap in the PLSR row finally got closed with a real SERS quantification study. And one ensemble row that quietly mixed two very different approaches got split into two, so the distinction reads honestly instead of looking like a duplicate.

show.event: three table rows appear: Random Forest, PLSR, Ensemble
Random Forest's mismatched citation is struck through and removed
PLSR's citation gap is filled with a real study
Ensemble row splits into two labeled rows

production_viz.label: three real table corrections
production_viz.mechanic: mock summary table with three live edits
production_viz.note: real fixes: mismatched citation removed, citation gap closed, row split for clarity

beats.narration_text: So: the draft started AI-generated and hollow, defining terms without ever explaining them. A guidelines document forced every section to answer what's been done, why it works or fails, and what to recommend. Two people split the sections, each running the same two-week cycle. Real citations replaced unsupported claims, a mismatched table row got caught and removed, and an honest admission replaced a number nobody could back up. That's what turning a draft into a real paper actually looks like.

props.artifactTitle: From a Draft to a Real Paper
artifactLines: The draft started AI-generated and hollow, defining terms without explaining them.
A guidelines document forced every section to answer what, why, and what to recommend.
Two people split the sections, each running the same two-week research-then-rewrite cycle.
Real citations replaced unsupported claims throughout the preprocessing and modeling sections.
A mismatched table citation was caught and removed; a long-open citation gap was closed.
An honest 'this hasn't been measured' replaced a specific-sounding number nobody could back up.

beats.narration_text: Your turn, ask Claude to read through your own writing and flag every claim that doesn't have a real citation backing it, the same way this rewrite did.
